{"id": "eb1fe155-97e9-4637-a7dc-b196e7f8b75f", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_o73w0BY47n6yNq5WRF9ygO", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Origin settings\",\"context\":\"## Connection timeout\\n\\nThe connection timeout is the number of seconds that CloudFront waits when trying to\\nestablish a connection to the origin. You can specify a number of seconds between 1 and\\n10 (inclusive). The default timeout (if you don\u2019t specify otherwise) is 10\\nseconds.\\n\\nUse this setting together with **Connection attempts** to specify how\\nlong CloudFront waits before attempting to connect to the secondary origin or before returning\\nan error response to the viewer. By default, CloudFront waits as long as 30 seconds (3\\nattempts of 10 seconds each) before attempting to connect to the secondary origin or\\nreturning an error response. You can reduce this time by specifying fewer attempts, a\\nshorter connection timeout, or both.\\n\\nIf CloudFront doesn\u2019t establish a connection to the origin within the specified number of\\nseconds, CloudFront does one of the following:\\n\\n* If the specified number of **Connection attempts** is more\\n than 1, CloudFront tries again to establish a connection. CloudFront tries up to 3 times, as\\n determined by the value of **Connection attempts**.\\n* If all the connection attempts fail and the origin is part of an origin group,\\n CloudFront attempts to connect to the secondary origin. If the specified number of\\n connection attempts to the secondary origin fail, then CloudFront returns an error\\n response to the viewer.\\n* If all the connection attempts fail and the origin is not part of an origin\\n group, CloudFront returns an error response to the viewer\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistValuesOrigin.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How do I increase the response and keep-alive timeout quotas for my CloudFront custom or VPC origin?\",\"context\":\"### Increase the response timeout and keep-alive settings for your CloudFront distribution\\n\\nTo increase how long CloudFront waits for a response from the origin, update the [response timeout](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistValuesOrigin.html#DownloadDistValuesOriginResponseTimeout) value. The default value is 120 seconds, but you can request a higher quota increase up to 180 seconds.\\n\\nTo maintain a longer connection to your custom origin after it gets the last response packet, increase the [keep-alive timeout](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistValuesOrigin.html#DownloadDistValuesOriginKeepaliveTimeout) value. The default keep-alive timeout value is 5 seconds, but you can increase the timeout value up to 180 seconds.\\n\\nComplete the following steps:\\n\\n1. Open the [CloudFront console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudfront/).\\n2. In the navigation pane, choose **Distributions**, and then select your distribution.\\n3. Choose the **Origins** tab, and then select your origin.\\n4. Choose **Edit**, and then expand **Additional settings**.\\n5. For **Response timeout**, enter the new timeout value.\\n6. For **Keep-alive timeout**, enter the new timeout value.\\n7. Choose **Save changes**.\\n\\n**Important:** If you receive \\\"HTTP 504\\\" errors from CloudFront, then see [HTTP 504 status code (Gateway Timeout)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/http-504-gateway-timeout.html)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/cloudfront-custom-origin-response\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Class CfnDistribution.OriginProperty\",\"context\":\"#### ConnectionAttempts\\n\\nThe number of times that CloudFront attempts to connect to the origin.\\n\\n```\\npublic Nullable<double> ConnectionAttempts { get; set; }\\n```\\n\\n##### Property Value\\n\\nSystem.Nullable<System.Double>\\n\\n##### Remarks\\n\\nThe minimum number is 1, the maximum is 3, and the default (if you don't specify otherwise) is 3.\\n\\nFor a custom origin (including an Amazon S3 bucket that's configured with static website hosting), this value also specifies the number of times that CloudFront attempts to get a response from the origin, in the case of an Origin Response Timeout .\\n\\nFor more information, see Origin Connection Attempts in the *Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide* .\\n\\n**Link**: http://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-properties-cloudfront-distribution-origin.html#cfn-cloudfront-distribution-origin-connectionattempts\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v1/dotnet/api/Amazon.CDK.AWS.CloudFront.CfnDistribution.OriginProperty.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify CloudFront origin default connection attempts/timeouts and review guidance"}

{"id": "8d264550-f48b-46ba-bd18-0ff10c560027", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "## Short answer: it depends on what the review is actually checking for

CloudFront's defaults are:

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| Connection attempts | 3 |
| Connection timeout | 10 seconds |
| Origin response timeout | 30 seconds |

These defaults aren't inherently "wrong" — plenty of well-run distributions use them as-is, and AWS doesn't flag defaults as a compliance violation on their own. Whether this "passes" an operational review depends on what the reviewer is actually assessing:

- **If the review is checking for intentional tuning based on origin behavior** (e.g., origins with longer processing times, or ones where fast failover matters), leaving everything at default can be flagged as a gap — it suggests the timeouts weren't evaluated against the origin's actual latency profile, which risks premature 504 Gateway Timeout errors for slow origins, or a slower-than-necessary failover (up to 30 seconds worst case) if the origin is actually unhealthy.
- **If the review is just checking that values are explicitly set and within valid/documented bounds**, defaults are fine and would pass.
- **If origin failover (origin groups) is in use**, relying on default connection attempts/timeout means CloudFront waits the full 30 seconds before failing over — many reviews flag this as something to tune down for faster failover.

So there's no single AWS-mandated pass/fail threshold tied to "using defaults" — it's a judgment call based on the origin's actual performance characteristics and failover requirements. If you want, I can look at the actual CloudFront distributions in your account and check whether their configured origins are using defaults or custom values, and flag any that look risky given their origin type.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
